question.problem: Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on the set $A={0,\,\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4},$ defined by $x∼y$ if ${x}^{2}={y}^{2}.$ How many distinct equivalence classes does $∼$ partition $A$ into?

current_example.problem: Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},$ defined by $a \sim b$ if $\textrm{i}^a = \textrm{i}^b,$ where $\textrm{i}$ is the imaginary unit in $\mathbb{C}.$  How many distinct equivalence classes does $\sim$ partition $A$ into?
current_example.worked_solution:
The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & ={a\in A∣a∼0} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{0}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=1} \\  & ={0,4,8} \\  \\ [1] & ={a\in A∣a∼1} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{1}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=\text{i}} \\  & ={1,5,9} \\  \\ [2] & ={a\in A∣a∼2} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=-1} \\  & ={2,6} \\  \\ [3] & ={a\in A∣a∼3} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}={\text{i}}^{3}} \\  & ={a\in A∣{\text{i}}^{a}=-\text{i}} \\  & ={3,7}\end{aligned}
$$

Each element of $A$ has been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $4$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$
[0] = \{ 0, 4, 8 \} , \quad [1] = \{ 1, 5, 9 \}, \quad [2] = \{ 2, 6 \}, \quad [3] = \{ 3, 7 \}.
$$
